summary:
Panama is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 2008 by presidential decree on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. No traveller-facing restrictions are in force: there are no bathroom or facilities laws, no documented inspection of gender markers at the border, and no recorded pattern of police targeting trans visitors.

Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery, and no nonbinary recognition is available. A visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with presentation has no documented record of friction at Panamanian entry points, though the surgery requirement shapes which documents residents are able to obtain in the first place.

No statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. The National Assembly blocked an amendment to the general anti-discrimination law in 2024, and no acts are formally recognised as hate crimes. At the 2025 Universal Periodic Review multiple states urged Panama to adopt explicit anti-discrimination protections, reform gender recognition and strengthen safeguards against violence. Those reforms remain stalled, leaving the country behind much of the wider hemisphere.

Same-sex marriage is not available. The Supreme Court ruled in March 2023 that marriage equality is not a constitutional right, following a 2017 draft ruling by Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega that found the family code's bars on same-sex marriage not unconstitutional while leaving the National Assembly to legislate civil unions. The government signalled in 2018 that it would comply with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision of 9 January 2018, but no implementing legislation followed.

Social hostility is moderate. Machista culture persists and trans women face documented employment exclusion, yet violent targeting remains well below Northern Triangle levels. Public approval of same-sex marriage stands at 12 percent, ranked 18th of 22 in the Americas by the AmericasBarometer 2023. Panama City has a visible, established trans community and hosts regional LGBT organising.
tangentialFactors:
Gender diversity is received unevenly across the country. In the Guna Yala indigenous territory a flourishing third-gender community, the Omeggid, is accepted as completely normal, and strong matriarchal figures elevate the status of women. Visitors moving between that territory and the capital should expect markedly different local attitudes to gender nonconformity.

The marriage litigation of 2017 and 2018 shows how organised the opposition remains. Two lawsuits, a suit seeking recognition of a foreign same-sex marriage and a direct challenge to the family code, were combined after oral arguments in the summer of 2017, with amicus briefs from regional marriage-equality advocates and public support from the First Lady, while Catholic and evangelical groups spearheaded opposition. A subsequent civil-union proposal came under attack from the Catholic Church.

Public opinion is a real constraint on reform. Only 12 percent of respondents approve of same-sex marriage, placing Panama 18th of 22 in the Americas on the AmericasBarometer 2023, and Outright International assesses the country as lagging much of Latin America on legal protections.

Blood donation carries an indefinite deferral for men who have sex with men, a rule that applies to visitors as well as residents.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition requires surgery, and no nonbinary marker is recognised, so residents must undergo a medical procedure to align civil documents with gender identity.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination in employment or housing on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The National Assembly's refusal in 2024 to amend the general anti-discrimination law to include these grounds, on the stated basis that coverage is already implicit, closed the main legislative route to such protection. Trans women face documented exclusion from employment as a result.

No acts are formally recognised as hate crimes, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted without a hate-crime enhancement. Conversion therapy is not banned. Surgeries on intersex infants are not prohibited and remain unregulated.

At the 2025 Universal Periodic Review several states urged Panama to adopt explicit anti-discrimination protections, reform the gender-recognition process and strengthen safeguards against violence targeting LGBT people. The government has not acted on those recommendations, and legal reforms remain stalled.

Men who have sex with men are subject to an indefinite deferral from blood donation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no reporting on whether Panamanian border officials inspect or question gender markers on passports. The absence of documented friction at entry is not evidence of a screening policy operating either way, and visitors carrying incongruent documents should treat the point as unresolved.

No sourced data exists on police handling of complaints from trans people, on recorded incidents of bias violence, or on prosecution outcomes. The finding that no acts are recognised as hate crimes describes legal status, not enforcement performance.

Whether the government's 2018 signal of compliance with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision produced any bill before the National Assembly is unresolved in the inventory, as is whether any civil-union mechanism currently exists in practice.

Equaldex records marriage as banned while the Supreme Court's March 2023 ruling is reported separately; the two are consistent on outcome but the inventory does not establish whether further litigation is pending.

Enforcement of the rules on intersex infant surgery, conversion therapy and blood donation is not sourced, and the practical availability of surgery-based gender recognition, including cost and waiting time, is not documented.
